posts.title: Carburettor ice on a warm day
posts.headline: Your carburettor makes its own cold, whatever the OAT.
posts.alt: Carburettor ice on a warm day: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your carburettor makes its own cold, whatever the OAT. The picture shows a rendered single-engine aeroplane in level cruise, small and high in the frame, over hazy summer farmland; a large cutaway of its carburettor filling the near foreground, sectioned along the induction path so intake mouth, venturi throat and throttle plate all read; pale streamlines entering the intake mouth and squeezing through the narrow throat, with the fuel spray leaving the nozzle in that same throat; a granular rime collar around the partly closed throttle plate, feathering thinner up the bore wall behind it. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: How does carburettor ice form when the outside air is well above freezing?

Fuel vaporising in the venturi absorbs heat, and the pressure drop through it cools the induction air further. The charge can end up below freezing. A warm OAT is what makes the risk easy to dismiss, and reduced power in humid air is when it shows up.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Fuel vaporisation and the pressure drop through the venturi cool the induction air substantially below ambient.
Carburettor ice is therefore possible at outside air temperatures well above freezing, particularly at high humidity and reduced power.
posts.intent: The temperature drop happens inside the carburettor, so ice forms on a day well above freezing.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 7

posts.title: Acceleration that feels like a climb
posts.headline: With nothing to see outside, speeding up feels like pitching up.
posts.alt: Acceleration that feels like a climb: an illustrated diagram for pilots. With nothing to see outside, speeding up feels like pitching up. The picture shows a rendered Cessna 172 in clean left profile, seen level and square to its flank, high wing with visible struts and fixed tricycle gear, its nose pitched clearly down below level; a translucent outline of the same aeroplane overlapping it and sharing its tail position, pitched clearly nose-high, so the picture reads as one aeroplane in two attitudes rather than as two aircraft; a wide, obvious angle between the two noses, the ghost's high and the solid one's low, which is the subject of the picture; a thin pale line tracing the aeroplane's real path: up off the runway, over a shallow crest, then bending down toward the unlit water. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Why does forward acceleration feel like a nose-up pitch attitude?

Accelerate forward with no outside references and your sense of pitch says the nose came up. It did not, and the correction it invites is lowering the nose toward the surface. Nothing outside can settle it, so fly the pitch on the flight instruments and disregard what your body is reporting.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: Forward acceleration can produce a false sensation of a nose-up pitch attitude.
Without outside visual references the pilot may lower the nose toward the surface, so pitch must be flown on the flight instruments rather than on what the body reports.
posts.intent: On a dark night takeoff, acceleration pushes the inner ear the same way a nose-up pitch would, and the instinct is to push down.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 17

figure_key.points_at: The raised nose and spinner of the translucent ghost aeroplane.

figure_key.label: PITCH YOU ACTUALLY HAVE
figure_key.points_at: The solid aeroplane's nose, visibly below the ghost's and below level.

figure_key.label: NO HORIZON TO CHECK IT
figure_key.points_at: The place straight ahead of the spinner where black water meets sky with no seam.

figure_key.label: FLY THE INSTRUMENTS

article.heading: What a dark takeoff feels like
paragraphs: You line up at night at a coastal airfield. Past the runway lights there is water, and past the water there is nothing lit at all. You push the throttle up and the aeroplane begins to accelerate.
A few seconds later your body reports that the nose has risen, and risen more than you set it. Everything you feel says steep climb. The flight instruments say otherwise.
The FAA handbook lists this one under climbing while accelerating. Gaining speed, on its own, can feel like pitching the nose up.

article.heading: Why speeding up feels nose-up
paragraphs: Start with what acceleration does to your body. As the aeroplane gains speed you are pressed back into the seat, and your back feels that push.

Now take the same seat and tilt the aeroplane nose-up. You are pressed back again, in much the same direction and much the same way. Your inner ear, the balance sense that tells you which way is up, gets a very similar push from both.

In daylight the argument ends at once, because you look outside and the horizon settles it. On a black night over water there is no horizon to look at. Nothing contradicts the sensation, so the sensation stands.

article.heading: Why the nose ends up down
paragraphs: A pilot who feels a steep climb does the reasonable thing about it. You ease the nose down to bring it back. Since the climb was never there, what you have really done is point the aeroplane lower.
That correction is worst in the first minute after takeoff. You are low, the surface below is unlit, and there is nothing outside to show the nose going down.
The handbook's own summary of these demonstrations is blunt about the body. Its read on the aeroplane's attitude is wrong often enough that you cannot use it.

figure.caption: The pilot corrects a climb that was never happening, and the real path bends down toward the water.
figure.alt: The pilot corrects a climb that was never happening, and the real path bends down toward the water.

article.heading: Meeting it with an instructor
paragraphs: You can meet this illusion on purpose, at height, with an instructor flying and looking outside. The handbook sets out the exercise. You close your eyes while the aeroplane is held straight and level at approach airspeed, the speed you would fly on final.

Then the instructor accelerates and holds that same straight and level attitude. With your eyes shut, what you usually feel is a climb. Opening them shows an aeroplane whose attitude has not changed at all.

Do not fly this at low altitude, and not without an instructor pilot or a safety pilot. There are also ground devices that produce these illusions with no aeroplane involved, such as a Barany chair or a Vertigon.

article.heading: Flying pitch on the instruments
paragraphs: With no horizon outside, your pitch comes off the flight instruments and nowhere else. That means reading them and acting on them while your body insists on something different. The instruction in the handbook is to trust the instruments and set the sensation aside.

The sensation itself does not go away. It is a normal thing for a pilot to feel, and training does not delete it. What training builds is the habit of flying the instruments anyway, and pilots who stay proficient on instruments are less affected.

So the work is done before the night takeoff, not during it. Get training and keep your proficiency in aircraft control by reference to the instruments before you fly where no horizon is evident. Over open water at night counts, and so does visibility less than 3 miles.

posts.title: Rotor cloud under a mountain wave
posts.headline: In a mountain wave, the roughest low-level air is under that smooth cloud.
posts.alt: Rotor cloud under a mountain wave: an illustrated diagram for pilots. In a mountain wave, the roughest low-level air is under that smooth cloud. The picture shows a mountain ridge in profile with the wind crossing it left to right; a smooth, hard-edged lens of lenticular cloud sitting at the wave crest downwind of the summit; a torn, ragged rotor cloud directly below that lenticular, at about ridge-top height; streamlines drawn unbroken from the lenticular down into the rotor, so the two clouds read as one wave. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: What's the difference between a lenticular cloud and a rotor cloud?

Air crossing a ridge can set up a standing wave downwind. Smooth lenticular cloud marks the crests. The rotor turns underneath, and down low that roll is usually the roughest part. The wave can be rough higher up too, so smooth cloud above is not a promise of smooth air.
Full explainer, and the FAA sources, at the link in our bio.
teaches: A mountain wave can form smooth lenticular cloud at its crests and turbulent rotor cloud beneath them.
At low level the rotor beneath the crests is usually the most turbulent part of the wave.
posts.intent: The smooth lenticular above and the ragged rotor below belong to the same wave, and down low the rotor is where the turbulence lives.

figure_key.label: SMOOTH EDGES MARK THE CREST
figure_key.points_at: The hard lit upper lip of the stacked lenticular cloud at the wave crest.

figure_key.label: ROTOR: USUALLY THE ROUGHEST
figure_key.points_at: The dark torn belly of the rotor cloud rolling directly beneath that lenticular.

figure_key.label: ONE WAVE, TWO DIFFERENT CLOUDS
figure_key.points_at: The streamline that runs unbroken from the lenticular crest down into the rotor roll.

posts.title: The fuel you cannot use
posts.headline: Usable fuel is less than your tanks hold.
posts.alt: The fuel you cannot use: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Usable fuel is less than your tanks hold. The picture shows a rendered low-wing single-engine aeroplane in level cruise, solid and fully lit, with a thin pale track line running forward from the spinner and stopping in open air; a translucent dimmed ghost of the same aeroplane further along that same track line, with open air between the solid aircraft and the ghost; a cut-away section through the wing fuel tank lifted large into the near foreground, joined to the wing root by one thin line; fuel brimmed to the filler neck inside that cut-away, its upper surface clearly the top of what the tank holds. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Usable fuel is less than your tanks hold.
Full explainer with the FAA sources it rests on flightdecide.com/e/fuel-cannot
teaches: An aircraft's total fuel capacity includes an unusable quantity that cannot be relied on in flight.
Fuel planning uses the usable figure from the approved flight manual.
posts.intent: Usable fuel is less than total fuel, and the difference is a published number rather than a rounding error.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 10
Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 7

figure_key.label: THIS IS TOTAL, NOT USABLE
figure_key.points_at: The brimmed fuel surface where it meets the filler neck at the top of the cut-away tank bay.

figure_key.label: TRAPPED BELOW THE PICKUP
figure_key.points_at: The thin separate band of fuel lying in the floor corrugations beneath the fuel pickup.

figure_key.label: TOTAL FUEL GETS YOU HERE
figure_key.points_at: The translucent dimmed ghost aeroplane further along the track line.

figure_key.label: PLAN FROM THIS FIGURE
figure_key.points_at: The ruled line in the fuel table on the open flight manual page.

article.heading: Why full tanks are not full
paragraphs: You top the tanks, watch the fuel rise to the filler neck, and call them full. Full is the tanks holding all they can. Some of what is in there will never reach the engine.
Fuel leaves the tank through a pickup, an opening the fuel line feeds from. That pickup sits a short way above the floor of the tank. Fuel lying below that opening has nothing there to draw it up.
So the tank carries two quantities at the same time. Total fuel is all of it. Usable fuel is the part the engine can be fed, and it is the smaller figure.

article.heading: Why engines quit with fuel aboard
paragraphs: Between the tank and the cylinders sits a pump, and pumps are built to move liquid. Once the fuel level drops below the pickup, the pump is drawing air. The engine gets nothing it can burn.

Picture the last of it sliding along the tank floor while the propeller winds down. That is fuel starvation, fuel aboard the aircraft that never arrives at the engine. The tanks are not empty. The engine is.

Some engines are fuel injected, with the fuel sprayed in at the cylinder intake ports. Others mix it with the incoming air in a carburetor first. Neither one can use fuel the pump cannot lift out of the tank.

article.heading: Where the real number lives
paragraphs: The flight manual approved for your aircraft gives the usable figure, and that is the one you plan with. It is a published number. Somebody wrote that figure into the table for this aircraft, and it is there to be read before you fly.
Find the fuel section of the manual and read the usable figure for your aircraft. Write it down before you work out anything else. Every later number in the plan rests on that one line.

The gap between the two figures is not slack in the measurement. It is a stated quantity for that aircraft. Treat it as a rounding error and your plan ends up counting on fuel you were told not to count on.

article.heading: What this changes in your planning
paragraphs: Run the numbers against total capacity and you've spent fuel that was never yours. It does not show up early. The shortfall turns up at the end of the leg, which is the worst end to find it.

The hours you can stay up and the distance you can cover both come off the usable figure. Start from the wrong one and every line after it is wrong by the same amount. The error travels all the way to the bottom of the page.
The unusable part has weight, and you carry it the whole flight. Weight aboard costs you performance whether or not you can burn it. So it belongs in the weight you plan, not in the fuel you plan.

posts.title: Ground effect in the flare
posts.headline: Your drag falls away inside the last wingspan.
posts.alt: Ground effect in the flare: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Your drag falls away inside the last wingspan. The picture shows a rendered light single nose-high in the flare, wings level, main wheels hovering a few feet above the runway centreline; a ticked vertical dimension line one wingspan tall from the low aircraft's wingtip to the asphalt, with the aeroplane sitting well inside it; ghost comparison: the same aeroplane in the same nose-high attitude, a pale unfilled outline about one and a half wingspans higher and slightly behind; tip trails behind the low aircraft pressed wide and shallow along the asphalt, while the ghost's trails curl into two deep, tight vortices. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Throttle closed, the nose where you set it, and the airplane keeps flying down the runway.
Come within a wingspan of the surface and the wing enters ground effect. Induced drag goes down. The airplane holds off, and the runway keeps going by.
The same thing happens on takeoff. You can be airborne below normal flying speed, then settle back as you climb out of the last wingspan.
FlightDecide computes your takeoff weight from the fuel you loaded.
Full explainer with the FAA sources it rests on https://flightdecide.com/explainers/ground-effect-in-the-flare/
When somebody asks why you floated, what is the one word in your answer?
teaches: Within about one wingspan of the surface, ground effect reduces induced drag and the thrust required to hold a low airspeed in level flight.
The reduced drag is why an aircraft floats in the flare and why it can lift off below normal flying speed and settle back.
posts.intent: Within about one wingspan of the surface induced drag falls away, so the aeroplane floats on air that has nowhere to go.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 5

figure_key.label: ONE WINGSPAN TO THE RUNWAY
figure_key.points_at: The thin vertical dimension line running from the low aircraft's left wingtip down to the asphalt.

figure_key.label: STILL FLOATING, THRESHOLD BEHIND YOU
figure_key.points_at: The band of daylight between the low aircraft's main wheels and the runway centreline.

figure_key.label: SAME ATTITUDE, STILL SINKING
figure_key.points_at: The pale ghost outline higher up and the two tight tip vortices trailing beneath it.

article.heading: Where ground effect starts
paragraphs: The last part of a landing happens in air that is behaving differently from the air you flew the approach in. Below about one wingspan above the surface, the wing no longer has open air underneath it. That band is called ground effect, and your own wings measure it out tip to tip.

A wing holds you up by pushing a mass of air downward. With the runway right there, that air has nowhere to go. The surface gets in the way of the flow around the wing, and the whole pattern of it changes.
Ground effect is strongest when you hold a steady attitude at low speed close to the surface. That is the flare. It is also the first seconds after lift-off.

article.heading: Why lift costs you drag
paragraphs: At each wingtip, the higher pressure under the wing leaks around to the lower pressure on top. The escaping air curls up over the tip, joins the downward flow behind the wing, and rolls into a spinning core called a vortex. One trails from each tip whenever the wing is lifting.

Spinning all that air takes energy, and the energy comes out of your forward motion. That is induced drag, the drag you pay for making lift. Raise the angle of attack, the angle between the wing and the oncoming air, and it grows.

A bigger angle means a bigger pressure difference and stronger vortices. Slow flight needs a high angle of attack, so induced drag is the drag that dominates down there. That is the speed you fly a flare at.

At cruise it is the other way round. Parasite drag, the cost of hauling the airframe through the air, is most of the total, and induced drag is a small part. Ground effect belongs to the two ends of the flight.

article.heading: What the ground takes away
paragraphs: Inside that last wingspan the wing's wake shrinks. The air it lifts ahead of itself, the air it pushes down behind, and the vortices at the tips are all reduced. Weaker vortices mean less induced drag.
The size of it is worth knowing. At a height equal to 1/4 of the span, induced drag drops by about 25 percent. At 1/10 of the span, it drops by about 50 percent.

So the wing needs a lower angle of attack in ground effect to make the same lift. Hold the attitude where it was and the wing makes more lift instead. Either way, the thrust needed to hold a low speed in level flight falls.

article.heading: Why you float
paragraphs: With the power at idle over the runway, drag is the only thing slowing you down. In the last wingspan a large share of that drag is missing. Your speed bleeds off slowly and the wing goes on flying.
Any extra speed you carry across the threshold has to be spent in there. Low speed is where induced drag would normally do that job. It is the drag the ground has just taken away.
The effect grows stronger the lower you get. The final few feet are where the airplane feels least willing to land.

article.heading: The same air on takeoff
paragraphs: The takeoff roll and the lift-off happen inside the same band of air. With induced drag reduced, the wing can pick the airplane up before it has the speed it needs to fly out of ground effect.

Climb out of the last wingspan and the help ends. Induced drag comes back, the thrust required goes up, and the wing needs a higher angle of attack to hold the same lift. An airplane that left the ground below flying speed can settle back onto the runway.

Leave below the recommended climb speed and the initial climb will be far weaker than it should be. Thin air from heat or field elevation, called high density altitude, makes that worse. So does maximum gross weight.
An airplane can lift off in those conditions and still be unable to climb out of ground effect. If there are obstructions off the far end, it may not clear them.

posts.title: A narrow runway and a low approach
posts.headline: A narrow runway hides how low you really are.
posts.alt: A narrow runway and a low approach: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A narrow runway hides how low you really are. The picture shows the runway seen obliquely ahead, its paved width visibly narrow with the edges close together and the markings small and crowded; a pale unfilled outline of the usual, wider runway drawn around the real one, so the gap between true edge and outline can be read; ghost outline of the same aeroplane on the normal approach path, at the same distance out and clearly above the solid one; solid aeroplane low on a shallower path, sitting close to the ground short of the threshold. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: You're on short final at a field you've never used, and the picture out the windscreen looks normal.

The runway ahead is narrower than the ones you learned on. A runway narrower than usual creates the illusion of extra height. That is the narrow runway illusion, and it needs nothing more than the width you're looking at. The picture says come down.

Miss it and the approach goes low. Objects along the approach path start to matter, and landing short is the other end of the same mistake. The Aeronautical Information Manual files it at 8-1-5, with the rest of the illusions of flight.
FlightDecide reads the NOTAMs for your destination and flags runway and obstruction notices in the briefing.
Next time you brief an unfamiliar field, look up its runway width and compare it to your home runway.
Check the current CFR before you apply this to a real flight.
teaches: A runway narrower than usual creates the illusion that the aircraft is higher than it actually is.
A pilot who does not recognise the illusion flies a lower-than-normal approach, with the risk of striking objects along the approach path or landing short.
posts.intent: A narrower runway than you are used to makes you feel higher than you are, and the uncorrected result is an approach that is too low.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 17

figure_key.label: LOWER THAN IT FEELS
figure_key.points_at: The solid aeroplane on the lower, shallower approach path.

figure_key.label: NOT THE WIDTH YOU KNOW
figure_key.points_at: The gap between the real runway edge and the pale outline of the usual width drawn around it.

figure_key.label: NORMAL PATH, UP HERE
figure_key.points_at: The ghost aeroplane on the upper, normal approach path.

figure_key.label: TREES IN YOUR PATH
figure_key.points_at: The conifer tops short of the threshold that the solid aeroplane's path grazes.

article.heading: Why a narrow runway feels high
paragraphs: Your eye learned a shape. Approach after approach at the same field, you built a picture of what a runway should look like from a normal glide path. You fly the approach against that picture.
Width is most of that picture. Take it to a narrower runway and the strip sits thinner in the windscreen. Thinner reads as higher.
What counts as usual is personal. A runway is narrow only against the ones your eye has been trained on, and that training shifts as you fly new fields.
The conditions do not have to be poor. This happens in clear air at a quiet airport, on an approach that is otherwise going well.

article.heading: The correction that puts you low
paragraphs: Feeling high, you correct. The aeroplane ends up on a path below the one you intended, and nothing in the windscreen objects.
The runway looks like a runway and the approach feels tidy. A small correction for apparent height feels like ordinary flying. Nothing in the aeroplane tells you the reference was wrong.
Each foot you lose makes the runway look a little more like the one you know. The descent feels like it is working.

article.heading: What a low approach runs into
paragraphs: A low path takes you close to the ground short of the runway. Trees that pass well beneath a normal approach do not pass beneath this one.
Sometimes nothing stands in the way. The path is still low, and it risks putting the wheels down before the pavement starts.
Neither outcome needs a second mistake. An approach that starts low stays low until you notice the height is wrong.

article.heading: Expect it at unfamiliar fields
paragraphs: Expecting the illusion takes most of its power away. An illusion you have already named on the ground has much less grip on you on short final.

A look from above is worth taking. Flying over an unfamiliar airport before you set up for landing shows you the runway from outside the approach picture. From up there the width is something you look at, rather than something you feel.
Your home field is not where this catches you. You have flown that width many times, and it set the standard your eye now uses.
Knowing the field is narrow changes what you do with the picture. It still looks wrong on final, and you can hold the normal path anyway, because you know why it looks that way.

article.heading: What to trust on final
paragraphs: An electronic glide slope or a VASI does the judging for you. Neither is reading the runway width, so neither is fooled by it.
Plenty of runways have neither. There you are back on the picture, and frequent landings keep your sense of a normal approach sharp.
The cue is height you did not expect. If you feel comfortably high on final at a field you have never used, the runway width is the first thing to check.

posts.title: The black hole approach
posts.headline: Over dark ground you fly lower than you think.
posts.alt: The black hole approach: an illustrated diagram for pilots. With nothing lit below, you fly lower than intended. The picture shows night side elevation with the lit runway small and far in the right third and the approach entering from the left; solid aeroplane on the lower, shallower path, visibly close to the dark surface short of the field; ghost outline of the same aeroplane on the intended path at the same distance out, clearly above the solid one; completely unlit ground or water between the aeroplane and the threshold, with no towns, roads or scattered lights. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: You turn final over the bay, and the only lights anywhere are the ones on the runway.

Night approaches over unlit terrain or water have a name. The black hole approach. The cues you use to judge height and distance are gone. No roads or rooflines under the nose. Only the runway lights, sitting out there alone.

On a lit approach the picture corrects you the whole way down. Over black ground it never updates. A small sink goes unchallenged. The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge files it with the visual illusions in chapter 17.
FlightDecide reads your destination NOTAMs for the planned window, runway lighting outages included.
If the ground below the approach shows nothing, what is left to tell you how high you are?
teaches: An approach over unlit terrain or water removes the visual cues normally used to judge height and distance.
The result tends toward an approach lower than intended.
posts.intent: With no lit features between you and the runway there is no visual slope information, so the approach is flown on an impression.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 17

figure_key.label: ONLY LIGHTS IN SIGHT
figure_key.points_at: The runway edge and threshold lamps at the right of the frame.

figure_key.label: NOTHING LIT DOWN HERE
figure_key.points_at: The open black water midway between the aeroplane and the threshold.

figure_key.label: LOW, AND STILL DESCENDING
figure_key.points_at: The solid aeroplane on the sagging path.

figure_key.label: WHERE YOU MEANT TO BE
figure_key.points_at: The ghost aeroplane sitting on the dashed constant slope, directly above the solid one.

article.heading: How you normally judge height
paragraphs: Fly a night approach into a town and the ground keeps telling you where you are. Streetlights, driveways and lit rooftops slide under the nose at a rate you already know. The runway sits inside all that light.

None of it is deliberate. Your eyes compare the runway against the lit ground around it, and against the roads and houses sliding past the side windows. Height and distance come out of that comparison. Take it away and the reading stops.

article.heading: Why dark ground hides the slope
paragraphs: Now put the same runway on the far side of a lake, or behind unlit farmland. The runway edge lights and the threshold lamps are the only light in the windscreen. Between you and them, nothing is lit.

Your peripheral vision, the wide outer part of your sight that reads movement, is getting nothing. The pattern that normally tells you how fast the ground is coming up is absent. So the approach gets flown on the lights alone.

A patch of lights at the far end of the dark is a poor ruler. It is hard to tell how far off it is, and harder to tell what angle you are seeing it from. That is the black hole approach, and it is a picture problem rather than a flying problem.

article.heading: Which way the error goes
paragraphs: The impression is that you are high. Nothing contradicts it, so it sits there while you make the reasonable correction for being high, which is to let the aeroplane down. The path ends up below the one you meant to fly.

Distance drifts the same way. Dark ground with only a few lights on it makes the runway look as though it is receding, further away than it really is. A town beyond the field on higher ground pulls you the same way.

The runway can also look tilted, sloping up or down when it is doing neither. You fly the picture in front of you, because that is all there is. In the worst case it ends in a landing short of the runway.

article.heading: What to fly instead
paragraphs: Find a slope you are not guessing at. A visual approach slope indicator is a light system beside the runway that shows whether you are on the correct angle. An electronic glide slope, the vertical guidance on an instrument approach, does the same job.
With neither on offer, fly the panel. Altitude and rate of descent do not care how dark the ground is. They hold a normal approach when the view will not.

Read the field before you start down. Knowing the layout and where the airport ends means the lights ahead arrive as something you were expecting. Expect the illusion at an unfamiliar airport at night.
If you are unsure how high you are, or where you are against the runway, go around. Doubt is the trigger by itself.

posts.title: Attention narrowing under fatigue
posts.headline: Fatigue narrows your scan before you feel impaired.
posts.alt: Attention narrowing under fatigue: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Fatigue narrows your scan before you feel impaired. The picture shows side elevation of a single-engine aeroplane in profile left of centre, late in the day, with layered ridgelines stepping back to the right into haze; a narrow pale-edged cone of attention opening forward from the cockpit, reaching only one small lit notch of rock at the shoulder of the pass; ghost comparison: a thin unfilled outline of a far wider cone from the same point, spanning nearly the whole forward view, the scan the pilot believes is being flown; terrain inside the narrow cone crisp and readable, everything between its edges and the ghost outline dimmed and softened into haze. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Fourth hour in the airplane, you copy a squawk code and look up to find the heading off the bug.

Fatigue does that. It degrades attention, and it takes away the ability to divide attention between two jobs. Whatever your hands are doing wins. The instrument you were watching a minute ago goes unwatched, and nothing announces it.

You can't feel the narrowing while it's happening. Chapter 2 of the Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge covers why fitness gets judged against a written checklist. The same tired brain does the self-assessment, and it reports back that everything is fine.
FlightDecide reads the TAFs and NOTAMs across your whole planned window, so late-day workload is visible early.
On a long day, the checklist is the only honest opinion in the cockpit.
teaches: Fatigue degrades attention and the ability to divide it between tasks.
The degradation is difficult to self-assess, which is why a checklist rather than a feeling is used to judge fitness.
posts.intent: Fatigue narrows the field of attention before it feels like impairment, so the scan stops covering what you think it covers.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 2

figure_key.label: ALL YOU ACTUALLY READ
figure_key.points_at: The lit notch of rock at the near shoulder of the pass, where the narrow cone of attention lands.

figure_key.label: WHAT YOU THINK YOU COVER
figure_key.points_at: The upper edge of the wide ghost outline spanning the forward view.

figure_key.label: TRAFFIC YOU NEVER SAW
figure_key.points_at: The small crossing aeroplane sitting in the dimmed band between the narrow cone and the ghost outline.

figure_key.label: DO NOT JUDGE BY FEEL
figure_key.points_at: The pilot's upright silhouette in the cockpit.

article.heading: Why the scan shrinks
paragraphs: Attention is not one supply that you either have or do not have. Part of it is the work of splitting attention across several jobs that all need some. Fatigue degrades both of those.
The task in front of you holds on to its share. The one you only glance at loses turns, and the gap between glances gets longer.
Nothing goes dark when that happens. The part of the view you take in gets narrower, and it narrows around whatever you are working on.
You go heads down to set up the approach. When you look up, the airplane has been in a slow left turn for longer than you would have allowed.

article.heading: Why self-assessment misses it
paragraphs: The degradation is difficult to judge from inside your own head. The judgement about whether you are fit to fly runs on the faculty the fatigue is degrading.
There is also nothing that presents as missing. A narrow scan returns a sharp read of a small area, and it reports nothing at all about the rest.
So the picture you hold of your own coverage stays wide while the coverage itself shrinks. You are working from the version you had on a rested morning flight.
Traffic is the plain case. It sits in the windscreen, outside the band you are sampling, and leaves nothing behind for you to remember afterwards.

article.heading: Where it costs the most
paragraphs: Workload is not level from taxi to shutdown. The tasks increase sharply in the landing phase, and that phase demands more precision and attention than cruise does.
It is also the phase that asks you to hold several jobs at once. You watch airspeed and path while you change configuration, work the radio and look for other airplanes.

The accident record is concentrated in the same places. Landing accounts for 24.1 percent of general aviation accidents and takeoff for 23.4 percent. Approximately 80 percent of all aviation accidents are related to human factors.
The hours that tire you out come before the approach, not after it. Your narrowest scan of the day and the busiest flying of the day arrive together.

article.heading: What to use instead
paragraphs: Fitness gets judged against a written checklist because the feeling is not evidence. A list asks you things you answer by counting and by looking at a clock.
Personal minimums work the same way. You set them in advance and build them into habit, so the number exists before you have to apply it.
A written answer will never tell you that you are sharp. It tells you whether you are inside a limit you drew while you could still see well enough to draw it.

posts.title: Stall speed rising with bank angle
posts.headline: Steepen a level turn and your stall speed rises.
posts.alt: Stall speed rising with bank angle: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A steeper level turn raises your stall speed. The picture shows a rendered single-engine aircraft heeled hard over in a steep turn, wings near sixty degrees of bank; the nose held on the horizon so the steep turn reads as level, not descending; a pale ghost of the same aircraft in a shallow bank, wings close to level; a thin level reference line joining solid aircraft and ghost at the same altitude. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Halfway around the steep turn the horn chirps, and the airspeed needle hasn't moved.

The wing is holding you up and hauling you around the corner at the same time. In a level turn, load factor grows with bank angle. Stall speed follows the square root of that load. Same airplane, higher number.

That number never shows up on the panel. The needle reads the same as it did wings level, so the margin feels unchanged. It has shrunk. The Airplane Flying Handbook works through steep turns in chapter 5.
FlightDecide computes the weight and balance for your planned load, so the gross weight behind your published stall speeds is a number you already have.
Next steep turns with your instructor, note the speed where the buffet starts and compare it to the wings level figure.
teaches: In a level turn load factor increases with bank angle.
Stall speed increases with the square root of the load factor, so a 60 degree level turn doubles the load and raises the stall speed by about 41 percent.
posts.intent: A level turn raises load factor and the stall speed rises with the square root of it, so a steep turn stalls at a higher speed.

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 5

figure_key.label: 60 DEGREES OF BANK
figure_key.points_at: The banked aeroplane's raised wingtip against the tilted horizon.

figure_key.label: 2 G ON THE NEEDLE
figure_key.points_at: The needle of the small round accelerometer face at lower right.

figure_key.label: STALL SPEED UP 41 PERCENT
figure_key.points_at: The upper amber stall mark on the small airspeed dial at lower right.

figure_key.label: 1 G, WINGS LEVEL
figure_key.points_at: The ghost aeroplane's level wings.

article.heading: What the wing has to do
paragraphs: You roll into a bank at altitude and hold your height. The wing now has two jobs. It still carries the weight of the airplane, and on top of that it has to bend your path into a circle.
Doing both takes more lift than flying straight took. You get that lift by pulling back. Back pressure raises the angle of attack, which is the angle at which the wing meets the oncoming air.
Steepen the bank and the wing needs more lift again. That is the chain the whole subject hangs on. Bank costs lift, and lift costs angle.

article.heading: Where the extra load comes from
paragraphs: Lift you add has to be felt somewhere. Load factor is the name for it. It compares the lift the wing is making with what the airplane weighs.
Wings level, that figure is 1 G. The wing lifts what the airplane weighs and no more. Steepen the bank in a level turn and the figure climbs with it.

The outward pull of a turn, which handbooks call centrifugal force, adds to the weight the wing has to support. Keep the ball centered and hold a level turn at 60 degrees of bank. The load factor is 2 G.

article.heading: Why the stall speed climbs
paragraphs: A wing stalls at an angle. Take the angle of attack far enough and the air stops following the top of the wing. Lift drops off hard at that point and the wing is stalled.

Every airplane has one angle where that happens, the stalling angle, somewhere around 16 to 20 degrees depending on the design. That angle does not move. Weight and load change the speed at which you reach it, and the angle stays put.

Load the wing to 2 G and it reaches that angle at a higher speed than it would at 1 G. The speed does not climb as fast as the load does. It goes up with the square root of the load factor, so doubling the load adds 41 percent.

article.heading: What the published number assumes
paragraphs: The stall speed in your handbook is one condition. It assumes 1 G flight at a given weight and flap setting. Change the load and you have changed what that number refers to.
In a level turn at 60 degrees of bank the wing is carrying 2 G. The speed that stalls it sits 41 percent above the book figure.
You are closer to the stalling angle there than you were wings level. The pull that held your altitude is what took you closer.

article.heading: Getting the angle back
paragraphs: The buffet, a shake you feel through the airframe, is one warning. The horn is the other. In a steep turn both arrive at a speed that reads fine on the dial.
Ease the back pressure. Lowering the angle of attack is what unstalls a wing, and it is the first thing to do at any bank angle.
Rolling out works on the cause. Less bank means less load factor, and less load brings the stall speed back toward the 1 G figure.

posts.title: Losing the headwind on final
posts.headline: A decreasing headwind costs airspeed and drops you below the path.
posts.alt: Losing the headwind on final: an illustrated diagram for pilots. A decreasing headwind costs airspeed and drops you below the path. The picture shows two wind layers divided by a soft shear seam: long streamlines above, short stubby ones below; a dashed intended glidepath running straight down to the runway threshold; the solid aircraft sitting beneath that dashed path, just after crossing the seam; a pale ghost of the same aircraft still on the dashed path at the same point along final. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Headwind loss on final arrives late in the approach, where you have the least altitude to spare.

On final you are low and committed to a path. The wing knows only the air moving over it right now. Pattern altitude is history. A headwind that weakens as you descend hands you a sink you never asked for.

It is easy to read the sag as your own flying. The air changed. The Airplane Flying Handbook covers this in its approach and landing chapter. The speed does come back. You are lower than you planned by the time it does.
FlightDecide reads the wind lines in your TAF for the planned window, including a low level wind shear group when the forecast carries one.
One sentence worth carrying down final: the speed sagged because the air changed, and the airplane is already going low.
teaches: A decreasing headwind with descent produces a momentary loss of indicated airspeed.
The aircraft sinks below the intended path, and getting the airspeed back does not by itself return it to the path.
The pilot must recover the path, promptly adding power and adjusting pitch to correct for the wind's effect on the descent.
posts.intent: Descending out of a stronger wind into a weaker one costs airspeed, and the aircraft sinks below the path while it recovers.

figure_key.label: HEADWIND WEAKENS WITH DESCENT
figure_key.points_at: The short stubby streamlines in the lower wind layer, beneath the shear seam.

figure_key.label: INDICATED AIRSPEED DROPS MOMENTARILY
figure_key.points_at: The nose of the solid aircraft at the point where it crosses the shear seam.

figure_key.label: AIRCRAFT SINKS BELOW PATH
figure_key.points_at: The vertical gap between the solid aircraft and the dashed intended glidepath above it.

posts.title: A temperature inversion trapping haze
posts.headline: The inversion that smooths the air also traps the haze below.
posts.alt: A temperature inversion trapping haze: an illustrated diagram for pilots. The inversion that smooths the air also traps the haze below. The picture shows a valley filled with dense haze whose top is cut off along one ruler-straight horizontal line; clean transparent air above that line with distant ranges still crisp and edged; a smoke column from a chimney that climbs vertically, stops dead at the line, and spreads sideways into a long level sheet; a small profile aircraft flying at the top of the haze with wings dead level. Flight training explainer from FlightDecide.
caption: Temperature inversions are stable layers, and stable air is what keeps the haze from clearing.

Vertical motion is what carries smoke and haze away. A stable layer has none, so it collects in the air you are looking through. Stability does all of it. The Aviation Weather Handbook covers inversions in chapter 18.

A smooth ride is easy to read as good conditions. It reports on mixing. With mixing suppressed, the haze underneath has nothing to lift it out and nowhere to go. Smooth air is what the trap feels like from inside.
FlightDecide reads the TAFs for your planned window and shows the forecast visibility and haze in a briefing you can check against raw data.
If the ride goes glassy and the horizon turns milky, one layer is doing both.
https://flightdecide.com iOS: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/flightdecide/id6761793626
teaches: A temperature inversion is a stable layer that suppresses vertical mixing.
Because mixing is suppressed, haze and smoke concentrate below the inversion while the air within it is smooth.
posts.intent: Smooth air and poor visibility arrive together, because the inversion that stops the mixing also traps what is in the air.

figure_key.label: INVERSION SUPPRESSES VERTICAL MIXING
figure_key.points_at: The height where the rising smoke column stops climbing and spreads sideways into a level sheet.

figure_key.label: SMOOTH AIR INSIDE THE LAYER
figure_key.points_at: The small profile aircraft flying wings-dead-level at the top of the haze, on the inversion line.

figure_key.label: HAZE TRAPPED UNDERNEATH
figure_key.points_at: The dense amber-brown murk filling the valley floor beneath that line.

figure_key.label: VISIBILITY LOST BELOW THE LID
figure_key.points_at: The far end of the valley below the line, where the ridges dissolve into grey with no edges left.

article.heading: What a temperature inversion is
paragraphs: Air normally gets colder as you climb away from the ground. An inversion is a layer where that order turns over, with warmer air lying above cooler air.

Forecasters judge a layer by what happens to a small parcel of air pushed up into it. Inside an inversion, that parcel arrives colder and denser than the air around it. Being heavier, it settles back to the level it came from.
A profile like that is classed as absolute stability. Every parcel you could test in the layer resists being lifted, whether it is saturated or not.

article.heading: Why the air stops mixing
paragraphs: Stability is a property of the air you are flying through, and it decides whether vertical motion grows or dies. A stable layer answers every upward nudge with a push back down. Motion that starts inside it does not get far.
Vertical motion is how low air and high air trade places. With that exchange shut off, the air under the layer stays under the layer.
The ride smooths out for the same reason. Bumps in the low levels are parcels rising and sinking, and a stable layer does not allow them to.

article.heading: Why the haze stays below
paragraphs: Haze and smoke go where the air goes. Carried upward, they spread through a deep column and thin out. Held down, they stay in the shallow slice of air near the surface.

Under an inversion the second case applies. Whatever was already in the low air remains there, and anything added to it joins the same shallow layer. Concentration climbs because the volume available to it has stopped growing.
That slice is the air you look through in the pattern and on a low cross country. How far you can see is set by how much has gathered in it, not by how clear the sky is overhead.

article.heading: What the smooth ride reports
paragraphs: Comfort in the cockpit is a readout of how little the air is moving up and down. It carries no information about what that same stillness has collected underneath you.
Both conditions come from one property of one layer. One layer damped the turbulence and stopped the ventilation at the same time.
Plan for the visibility to be poorest on the mornings the air feels best. A glassy climb out of a valley is a reason to check the reported visibility again, not a reason to relax about it.

article.heading: When the trap lets go
paragraphs: Stability follows how fast temperature falls with height. Steepen that fall and stability drops.

Sun on the ground warms the air in contact with it, which steepens the profile from below. Once the heating has worked up through the layer, vertical motion returns. The load of haze then has a much deeper column to spread through.
Heating is not the only lever. Most changes in stability come from air moving in from somewhere else, so a layer can be built or broken by what arrives aloft.

posts.title: Lee-side downdraft
posts.headline: The air can sink faster than you can climb.
posts.alt: Lee-side downdraft: an illustrated diagram for pilots. The air can sink faster than you can climb.
caption: Lee-side downdraft: pitched up at climb power, an aircraft can still be losing height.

You plan a ridge crossing around climb performance. Descending air on the lee side can take that margin back, and FAA-H-8083-28 chapter 16 covers that flow. The margin goes first. The height goes next.
It is easy to read the attitude as proof of a climb. Pitch and power are inputs. The altimeter is the output. A steady nose-up picture can sit on top of a descending trend for the whole crossing.
FlightDecide computes the weight and balance for your planned flight window, which is one input to the climb performance you will have on the day.
If the nose is up and the altimeter is unwinding, believe the altimeter.
teaches: On the lee side of a ridge the air can be descending, and it can descend faster than a light aircraft climbs.
So a climb attitude does not guarantee a climb: the aircraft can be pitched up, at climb power, and still losing height.
posts.intent: air spilling down the downwind side of a ridge can descend faster than a light aircraft can climb, even at a climb attitude

article.heading: Why the air sinks there
paragraphs: The wind does not stop at the ridge. When the air is stable and the wind is strong, the whole layer gets lifted over the top.
Gravity pulls it back down, and it does not stop at the level it came from. Momentum then carries it well below that height before it begins to rise once more.
That descending stretch is the lee-side downdraft. It sits on the downwind side, right where you are still trying to climb.

article.heading: Climbing through air that is falling
paragraphs: Your climb rate is measured against the air around you, not against the ground. When that air is sinking faster than you climb, your height falls while the wing keeps climbing.
A light aircraft does not have a large climb rate to spend. Set a descending air mass against it and the sum can come out below zero. You sink.
Nothing in the cockpit picture changes while this happens. The attitude holds and the airspeed sits where you put it. Only the vertical speed and the terrain ahead tell you anything is wrong.

article.heading: When a ridge makes waves
paragraphs: A wave needs strong wind and stable air upwind of the ridge. Take away either one and the air behaves in another way.

Weak wind can leave the mountains acting as a dam, holding the air back on the upwind side. Unstable air that carries enough moisture tends to build convective cloud rather than a smooth wave. Neither of those is the lee-side case.
Season matters. Late autumn through early spring is when the large-scale winds run strongest, and that is when the worst mountain wind events show up.

article.heading: Where the sinking air sits
paragraphs: The descending air is part of a wave, so it repeats. Past the first trough the air swings back up and then overshoots once more. The oscillation fades downstream.

That gives you bands of sinking air separated by bands of rising air. Crossing them, the vertical speed swings one way and then the other. One good climb through a rising band does not mean the sink is behind you.
The handbook names two shapes for this. A vertically propagating mountain wave and a trapped lee wave can both be present, and each can be hazardous. The name matters less than the sink.

article.heading: What you might see first
paragraphs: Sometimes the flow announces itself. Lenticular cloud and blowing dust mark mountain flow that is under way. Rotor cloud under the wave is another sign.
The handbook is direct about the other case, where severe wind events happen with little or no visual warning. A clear sky over a ridge is not a promise that the lee side is quiet.
The ridge bends the wind and breaks it into eddies at the same time. Those run from a few centimeters to tens or hundreds of kilometers across. The ride through them can be smooth or violent.

posts.title: Wind correction angle
posts.headline: Line up with where you are going, not where you are pointing.
posts.alt: Wind correction angle: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Line up with where you are going, not where you are pointing.
caption: Wind correction angle is what keeps your track on the extended centreline in a crosswind.

In a crosswind your heading and your track over the ground are two different things. The angle between them is the wind correction angle. On final, hold it into the wind. The track then stays down the extended centreline. The crab comes out before touchdown, so the aeroplane lands with its longitudinal axis on the runway.
It is easy to read a nose pointed straight at the runway as lined up. You drift when the correction is missing. Chapter 16 of FAA-H-8083-25 lays out the same wind triangle for cross country legs.
FlightDecide pulls wind direction and speed from the TAF for your planned window, then scores it in the go/no-go advisor.
On the next crosswind final, notice how far off the runway heading your nose sits while the track stays straight.
teaches: In a crosswind an aircraft's heading and its track over the ground are different, and the angle between them is the wind correction angle.
On the approach, holding a wind correction angle into the wind is what keeps the track along the extended centreline.
An aircraft that points straight at the runway in a crosswind, with no correction applied, drifts downwind of the centreline.
Taking the crab out the instant before touchdown aligns the axis with the runway, but aileron into the wind stops the drift.
posts.intent: in a crosswind the aeroplane's nose points off to one side while its path over the ground stays on the centreline

posts.title: Density altitude
posts.headline: Thin air lengthens your takeoff and flattens your climb.
posts.alt: Density altitude: an illustrated diagram for pilots. Thin air lengthens your takeoff and flattens your climb.
caption: Density altitude takes thrust from the propeller and lift from the wing, and the runway does not grow.

Heat and elevation both thin the air. The field that felt long at seven in the morning is a different field at three in the afternoon. Your loading has not changed and neither has your technique. The ground roll grows anyway.

It is easy to treat runway length as the whole question. The climb gradient available is reduced on that same afternoon, and the rising ground past the departure end is still there. FAA-H-8083-25 chapter 11 has the performance side of this.
FlightDecide reads the TAF for your planned window and the weight and balance you entered, then scores both in one advisory.
After the longer ground roll, what is the other half of a density altitude problem?
teaches: Heat and elevation both thin the air, and thin air reduces the thrust the propeller makes and the lift the wing makes at a given speed.
Takeoff distance therefore grows with density altitude while the aircraft, its weight and the pilot's technique are all unchanged.
Rising terrain beyond the runway matters more on a thin-air day, because the climb gradient available is reduced at the same time as the ground roll is lengthened.
posts.intent: the same aeroplane uses far more runway to get airborne when the air is thin than when it is dense

citations.title: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25), Chapter 11

article.heading: Why thin air costs you
paragraphs: Air gets thinner for two reasons. Climb higher and there is less atmosphere left above you, pressing down. Heat the air and it expands, spreading the same molecules over more room.

Your engine breathes that air, and a thinner charge makes less power. The propeller has less to push against, so it turns that power into less thrust. The wing, meeting fewer molecules per second at the same speed, makes less lift.
All three losses come from one cause and show up together. Density altitude is how that single cause gets written down as a number.

article.heading: Why heat acts like height
paragraphs: Warm air expands and cool air contracts. Picture three columns of air with the same pressure at the bottom and the top of each. The warm one stands tallest, because expansion has stretched it.

Stretching a column spreads its air over more height, which leaves less of it down low where you are rolling. Elevation does the same job by a different route. Station pressure at Denver is lower than at New Orleans before temperature has had any say.
So a hot day and a high field are not two separate problems. They push the same way, and they can arrive together.

article.heading: Where the extra roll comes from
paragraphs: Less thrust means slower acceleration, so every knot takes longer to gain. Lift is also down at any given speed, so the aeroplane leaves the ground later than it would in denser air. Both of those get paid for in concrete.
Nothing about the aeroplane accounts for it. The weight is what you loaded, the flap setting is what you chose, and the technique is the one you always use. The distance grows on the air alone.

article.heading: The climb you have left
paragraphs: The same thinness that lengthened the roll takes away climb gradient. Reduced thrust and reduced lift do not stop mattering at the moment the wheels come up.
So the two effects compound. You leave the ground further down the runway, then climb away more shallowly from that later point. Both put you lower over anything that rises ahead.
Rising ground past the departure end has not moved. Your gradient has, and that is what narrows the gap between the two.

article.heading: Where your own numbers live
paragraphs: Generalities stop here. The performance section of your AFM or POH holds the takeoff and climb figures for the aeroplane you fly. The handbook treats the use of that data as mandatory for safe and efficient operation.

It is not presented the same way by every manufacturer. Some print tables and some print graphs. The basis differs too, and a chart may be built on standard conditions, on pressure altitude, or on density altitude.
Read the basis before you read the distance off it. A figure pulled from a chart whose basis you never checked is worth very little, whatever it says.
